## Preface

Natural gradient descent has a beautiful geometric story. Ordinary gradient descent measures a step in the coordinates in which the parameters happen to be written. Natural gradient descent instead measures a step by the change it induces in the model distribution.

The local ruler is the Fisher information matrix. For a parametric predictive model \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\),

$$
F(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_x\,\mathbb E_{y\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
\left[
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y\mid x)
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y\mid x)^\top
\right].
$$

The damped natural-gradient step is

$$
\theta_{t+1}
=
\theta_t
-
\eta\{F(\theta_t)+\lambda I\}^{-1}\nabla_\theta L(\theta_t).
$$

This is the right object to study if the question is information geometry rather than merely curvature. A Hessian-preconditioned method may be useful, but it is not natural gradient unless the Fisher metric is actually computed or approximated.

The point of this note is not that natural gradient or K-FAC is bad. The point is narrower:

> A correct local Fisher metric does not guarantee selection of the globally desirable basin in a multimodal non-convex likelihood.

This matters because many demonstrations of natural-gradient methods concentrate on benign cases, where the Fisher geometry is helpful and the good basin is already the basin suggested by the local metric. Edge cases are less flattering, but they are useful because they show what the method is not promising.

The recurring theme is the same as in the previous notes: geometry helps, but only at the level at which the geometry is defined. Fisher information gives a local geometry on a statistical model. It is not, by itself, a global map of the validation landscape.

## Part I: The information-geometric view

Let \(P_\theta\) denote the probability law induced by the model. If \(\theta\) and \(\theta+d\theta\) are close, then

$$
\mathrm{KL}(P_\theta\,\|\,P_{\theta+d\theta})
=
\frac12\,d\theta^\top F(\theta)d\theta
+
o(\|d\theta\|^2).
$$

Thus \(F(\theta)\) is the metric tensor associated with infinitesimal KL distance. A displacement \(v\) in parameter space has squared statistical length

$$
\|v\|_{F(\theta)}^2
=
v^\top F(\theta)v.
$$

Natural gradient is the steepest descent direction under this Fisher geometry. Equivalently, it is the solution of the local trust-region problem

$$
\min_{\Delta}
\left\{
\nabla L(\theta)^\top \Delta
+
\frac{1}{2\eta}\Delta^\top F(\theta)\Delta
\right\}.
$$

When \(F(\theta)\) is nonsingular, the solution is

$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{NG}}
=
-\eta F(\theta)^{-1}\nabla L(\theta).
$$

This form makes the promise and the limitation visible. The Fisher matrix tells us which infinitesimal steps are large or small in distribution space. It does not tell us which faraway basin has better validation loss.

### A measure-theoretic view

There is also a useful Hilbert-space way to read the same formula. For a dominated model with density \(p_\theta(z)\), write the score as

$$
s_\theta(z)
=
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(z).
$$

Under regularity conditions,

$$
\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[s_\theta(Z)]=0,
$$

so each score component is an element of the mean-zero space \(L_0^2(P_\theta)\). The Fisher matrix is the Gram matrix of these score functions:

$$
F_{rs}(\theta)
=
\left\langle
\partial_r\log p_\theta,
\partial_s\log p_\theta
\right\rangle_{L^2(P_\theta)}.
$$

A parameter velocity \(v\in\mathbb R^p\) maps to the tangent random variable

$$
z\mapsto v^\top s_\theta(z),
$$

and its squared norm is

$$
\mathbb E_{P_\theta}\{v^\top s_\theta(Z)\}^2
=
v^\top F(\theta)v.
$$

So natural gradient is not just “rescaling by a matrix.” It is steepest descent after measuring parameter motion by the \(L^2(P_\theta)\) norm of the induced score perturbation. That is the information-geometric content.

But it is still local. The inner product is taken under the current model \(P_\theta\). It is a statement about infinitesimal motion around the current distribution, not a global statement about the topology of the loss surface.

This is the distinction the experiment below is designed to expose:

- Fisher geometry can make the local direction better scaled.
- Fisher geometry does not solve global basin selection.

## Part II: The experiment

The experiment uses a two-parameter Bernoulli model

$$
p_\theta(y\mid x)
=
\mathrm{Bernoulli}\{\sigma(f_\theta(x))\},
\qquad
\theta\in\mathbb R^2.
$$

The logit \(f_\theta(x)\) is nonlinear in \(\theta\), so the validation surface over \((\theta_1,\theta_2)\) can have multiple basins. The point is not that this is a realistic large model. The point is that it is small enough to draw the surface and compute the exact Fisher matrix.

For a Bernoulli logit model, let

$$
p_i(\theta)=\sigma(f_\theta(x_i)),
\qquad
J_i(\theta)=\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x_i).
$$

The exact model Fisher on the training inputs is

$$
F(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
p_i(\theta)\{1-p_i(\theta)\}
J_i(\theta)J_i(\theta)^\top.
$$

This is not a Hessian proxy. It is the Fisher matrix of the predictive Bernoulli model.

I compare five optimizers:

1. AdamW;
2. SGD with momentum;
3. exact Fisher natural gradient;
4. empirical Fisher natural gradient;
5. diagonal exact Fisher.

The initializations are separated into three regimes.

- **Easy** starts are positive controls. The good validation basin is nearby, and all methods should have a fair chance.
- **Medium** starts are ambiguous. The good basin is reachable, but the trajectories can differ.
- **Hard** starts are adversarial. They are included to show failure modes, not to pretend that every start is equally reasonable.

This split is important. Without positive controls, the experiment would only say that the surface is hard. With easy, medium, and hard starts separated, the question becomes more precise: when the good basin is reachable, does Fisher geometry guarantee that it is selected?

### Endpoint classification

The endpoint labels are defined on the validation landscape. A run is counted as successful only if its final point lands in the good validation basin: the basin containing the best validation grid point. Endpoints that converge to other stable regions, or to stationary regions outside the good basin, are not counted as successes.

This is an empirical basin classification, not a theorem. It is deliberately stricter than reporting the final training loss. The question is not whether the optimizer made progress. The question is whether it selected the basin we wanted.

## Part III: Success rates by regime

The first figure summarizes the endpoint classification.

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Good-basin hit rate by initialization regime. Easy starts are positive controls; medium starts are the informative regime; hard starts expose failure modes.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_success_rate_by_regime.png)
:::

The easy starts do what they should do: they show that the task is not broken. Natural gradient, AdamW, SGD, and the diagonal Fisher method can all reach the good basin when the start is favorable.

The medium starts are more interesting. The good basin is not unreachable, but not all methods select it from every ambiguous start. This is the regime that tests the slogan. The local Fisher metric may be correct and still not encode the global basin structure.

The hard starts are a stress test. They should not dominate the interpretation, but they are useful because they show how local preconditioning can be pulled into an undesirable attractor just like first-order methods can.

Aggregating over all starts gives a compact comparison, but it should be read only after the regime split.

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Good-basin hit rate by optimizer, pooled over the balanced easy, medium, and hard starts.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_success_rate_by_optimizer.png)
:::

The pooled number is not the theorem. The more important observation is that the outcome depends on the starting regime. There is no single optimizer that turns local geometry into a global guarantee.

## Part IV: The trajectories

The level-set plots make the basin story more concrete. Line color and line style identify the optimizer. The final marker identifies the endpoint class.

The easy case is the sanity check.

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Easy initialization. All methods reach the good validation basin.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_landscape_easy_init0.png)
:::

This plot is useful because it prevents the experiment from becoming an anti-natural-gradient caricature. Exact Fisher NGD can work. The geometry can be helpful. The positive-control regime exists.

The medium cases are the real diagnostic.

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Medium initialization. The good basin is reachable, but the selected basin depends on the optimizer and the induced trajectory.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_landscape_medium_init2.png)
:::

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Another medium initialization. The local direction field can agree with the geometry and still not imply universal dominance.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_landscape_medium_init3.png)
:::

In these plots, the question is not whether Fisher information is wrong. It is locally correct by construction. The question is whether local correctness determines the global attractor. It does not.

The hard case is included as an edge case, not as the whole story.

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Hard initialization. Most methods are pulled toward bad or stationary basins.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_landscape_hard_init4.png)
:::

The hard plot should be read cautiously. If every plot looked like this, the experiment would only show that the initialization is too adversarial. Its role is different: it demonstrates that the local metric does not prevent bad-basin capture.

## Part V: Alignment is a diagnostic, not the conclusion

A tempting diagnostic is to compute the cosine alignment between the update direction and the direction to the best validation grid point. This is useful, but raw alignment curves are visually noisy and can be misleading. A single step can point locally away from the final target while still following a sensible curved path.

For that reason I prefer two summaries.

First, distance to the best validation grid point:

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Distance to the best validation grid point for one medium initialization. This is often easier to read than raw alignment.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_distance_medium_init2.png)
:::

Second, the cumulative fraction of steps with positive alignment:

::: {.narrow-figure}
![Cumulative fraction of steps whose update direction has positive alignment with the direction to the best validation grid point.](./figures/exact_fisher_2d_alignment_positive_rate_medium_init2.png)
:::

These plots are not meant to prove a theorem. They are diagnostics for the trajectory. They show that a method can make many locally plausible steps without being guaranteed to choose the desired basin.

## Part VI: Where K-FAC enters

The two-dimensional experiment is useful because the exact Fisher can be computed and the basins can be drawn. K-FAC enters as the neural-network analogue of the same idea: approximate the Fisher geometry with a structured local preconditioner.

For a linear layer with input activations \(a\) and preactivation score gradients \(\delta\), K-FAC approximates the Fisher block by

$$
F_l
\approx
A_l\otimes G_l,
$$

where

$$
A_l=\mathbb E[aa^\top],
\qquad
G_l=\mathbb E[\delta\delta^\top].
$$

The corresponding preconditioned weight-gradient has the form

$$
\Delta W_l
\propto
-
G_l^{-1}(\nabla_{W_l}L)A_l^{-1},
$$

with damping in practice.

This is a genuine Fisher approximation, not a Hessian trick. But it remains local. The Kronecker factors describe the local geometry of each layer. They do not, by themselves, decide which distant basin should be selected.

So the K-FAC lesson should be read as an analogy, not as a claim that the two-parameter experiment is a full neural-network benchmark. The common point is that Fisher-based methods are local metric-based methods. They can improve local scaling without guaranteeing the global basin.

## Technical appendix

### Exact Fisher for the Bernoulli model

Let

$$
p_\theta(x)=\sigma(f_\theta(x)).
$$

For one observation, the log-likelihood score is

$$
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y\mid x)
=
(y-p_\theta(x))\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x).
$$

Taking expectation over

$$
y\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_\theta(x))
$$

gives

$$
\mathbb E_y[(y-p_\theta(x))^2]
=
p_\theta(x)\{1-p_\theta(x)\}.
$$

Therefore

$$
F(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_x
\left[
p_\theta(x)\{1-p_\theta(x)\}
\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)
\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)^\top
\right].
$$

This is the matrix used by exact Fisher NGD in the two-parameter experiment.

### Model Fisher versus empirical Fisher

The model Fisher takes the inner expectation over labels drawn from the model itself. The empirical Fisher replaces that expectation with the observed labels. For the Bernoulli case, this gives

$$
\hat F_{\mathrm{emp}}(\theta)
=
\frac1n\sum_i
(y_i-p_\theta(x_i))^2
J_i(\theta)J_i(\theta)^\top.
$$

The two matrices can behave differently away from a well-specified optimum. That is why the experiment includes both exact Fisher NGD and empirical Fisher NGD.

### Damping and step size

All Fisher inverses in the experiment are damped:

$$
\{F(\theta)+\lambda I\}^{-1}.
$$

Damping is not a cosmetic implementation detail. Near singular regions, the Fisher matrix can be poorly conditioned, and the undamped inverse can produce unstable steps. Damping interpolates between natural gradient and ordinary gradient descent. It is therefore part of the optimizer, not merely numerical hygiene.

This also reinforces the main point. A damped Fisher step is a local metric step with a chosen trust scale. It can be excellent, but it is still not a global basin-selection rule.

### What the experiment is not claiming

This is not a no-free-lunch theorem. It is not a claim that AdamW is better than natural gradient in general. It is not a claim that K-FAC is only useful in easy cases.

It is a smaller diagnostic:

1. define a probabilistic model so that Fisher information is real;
2. compute exact Fisher NGD in the two-parameter case;
3. compare with empirical Fisher and diagonal Fisher variants;
4. separate easy, medium, and hard initialization regimes;
5. report endpoints rather than only scalar loss.

The resulting lesson is about guarantees. Fisher geometry gives a principled local ruler. It does not remove the global basin-selection problem.

## Takeaway

The careful claim is not:

> Natural gradient fails.

The careful claim is:

> Natural gradient and K-FAC are local metric-based methods. The Fisher metric may be the correct local geometry and still be globally uninformative about which basin is desirable.

This is why endpoint classification matters. A low loss, a short Fisher step, or a locally natural direction is not the same thing as reaching the basin one wanted. In non-convex problems, the optimizer is not only solving a local quadratic problem. It is generating a trajectory.

The practical question is therefore:

> Does the local geometry point toward the basin that matters for the task?

When the answer is yes, Fisher methods can be excellent. When the answer is no, there is no general reason to expect them to dominate AdamW.
